questions.question: Who should close a Go channel, and when should it be closed?
questions.title: Channel closing ownership
questions.direct_answer: The sending side should close a channel when it can prove that no more values will ever be sent. Closing announces the end of a stream; it is not required for garbage collection and is not a receiver's acknowledgment. With multiple senders, a coordinator should wait for all senders and close once—never let competing senders guess.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding that close is a one-time lifecycle event owned by the side that knows sending is complete.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Closing from a receiver or one of several producers while another producer may still send.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe the multiple-sender coordinator pattern and separate stream completion from cancellation.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Close means no future values will be sent on that channel.
The side that owns sending completion should call `close`.
Sending after close and closing twice both panic.
A coordinator can wait for multiple senders and perform the single close.
Do not close merely to release memory; unreachable channels are garbage-collected.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Closing a channel is a broadcast statement that the value stream is complete. The correct owner is the sending side that can prove no future send will happen. Receivers usually cannot know that fact, so they should not close a channel just because they are finished reading.

With one producer, that producer can `defer close(out)` and return after its last send. With several producers sharing one output, no individual producer knows whether the others are finished. A coordinator waits for all of them, commonly with a `sync.WaitGroup`, and closes the output exactly once after `Wait` returns.

For example, two workers can each send subtotals. A third goroutine waits for both workers and closes the results channel. The consumer safely ranges until close and never races with a late sender. Closing early would make that sender panic; closing from two places could also panic.

Close is not cancellation and not cleanup for garbage collection. It tells receivers that no more values are coming. If producers must stop because the consumer is leaving, I use context or a done signal as a separate protocol and make every blocking send observe it.

sections.title: Close is a proof obligation
sections.content:
The decisive question is not “who has the channel variable?” but “who knows the final send has completed?” That knowledge may belong to one producer or to a coordinator that tracks all producers. Keeping the close at that ownership point removes the need for recover, shared flags, or timing guesses.

Closing wakes receivers because the end-of-stream state is permanent. It does not interrupt arbitrary work and it cannot be undone. This makes close a good completion signal for a finite stream, but a poor substitute for request cancellation. A channel that carries isolated request-response values often does not need to be closed at all when receivers already know the exact count.

sections.title: Safely close after multiple producers
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P1[Producer 1] -- values --> R[results channel]
  P2[Producer 2] -- values --> R
  P1 -- Done --> W[WaitGroup]
  P2 -- Done --> W
  W -- Wait returns --> C[Coordinator closes results]
  R --> X[Consumer ranges until close]
  C --> R
```

questions.question: What does receiving from a closed Go channel return?
questions.title: Receiving buffered values and detecting closure
questions.direct_answer: A receive from a closed channel first returns any values sent before closure. After that buffer is drained, receives complete immediately with the element type's zero value. In `value, ok := <-ch`, `ok` is `true` for a sent value and `false` for the zero value produced because the channel is closed and empty.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to distinguish a real zero value from the closed-and-drained state.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating a zero value as proof of closure or reading forever without checking `ok`.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that buffered data survives close and why range uses the same termination condition.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Closing does not discard values already in the channel buffer.
Buffered values are received normally with `ok == true`.
After draining, receive returns the element zero value and `ok == false` immediately.
Use the two-value receive when zero is a valid payload and closure matters.
Repeated receives after draining keep returning zero and `false`.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Closing stops future sends, but it does not erase values already sent. A receiver drains the existing buffer in normal FIFO order. Each of those receives returns `ok == true` because the value came from a send that completed before closure.

Once the channel is closed and drained, a receive no longer blocks. It returns the element type's zero value and `false` in the comma-ok form. For an integer channel that means `0, false`; for a pointer channel it means `nil, false`. Repeating the receive gives the same closed result.

For example, if a buffered integer channel contains a deliberately sent zero and is then closed, the first receive is `0, true`. The next receive is also zero but has `ok == false`. Checking only the value cannot tell those events apart.

I use `value, ok := <-ch` when I need one receive and must distinguish completion. A `for value := range ch` loop performs the repeated receive pattern and stops at the closed-and-drained state. Either way, closure is a protocol event, not an error value hidden inside the data.

sections.title: Close adds an end state to the stream
sections.content:
An open channel represents a stream that may still receive future sends. Closing makes “no more sends” permanent while preserving the queue. This lets producers finish independently of the consumer's exact speed: the consumer can drain later and still recognize the endpoint.

The zero value is required because every receive expression must produce a value of the channel's element type. The Boolean supplies the missing origin information. It distinguishes a value actually transmitted by a sender from the synthetic zero returned after completion. APIs should not reserve a data value such as `-1` or an empty string as their close marker when the channel already has this separate state.

sections.title: Buffered close trace
sections.content:
| Step | Channel state | Receive result |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | Buffer contains sent `0`; still open | Not read yet |
| 2 | Channel is closed; buffer still contains `0` | Not read yet |
| 3 | Closed; sent value is drained | `0, true` |
| 4 | Closed and empty | `0, false` |
| 5 | Still closed and empty | `0, false` again |

sections.title: Distinguish a sent zero from closure
sections.content:
```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    values := make(chan int, 1)
    values <- 0
    close(values)

    first, firstOK := <-values
    second, secondOK := <-values
    fmt.Println(first, firstOK)
    fmt.Println(second, secondOK)
}
```
The output is `0 true` followed by `0 false`. The Boolean—not the numeric value—identifies closure.
